intro: Nishio maps one tree, and most of the original is no longer alive. Shinmeisha no Oshii stands in front of the main hall of Kaminagara Shinmeisha, an evergreen chinquapin put at about a thousand years old whose main trunk has died and whose two secondary trunks and root suckers have carried on without it. Twenty metres round at the roots, eight metres tall, the largest of its species in Aichi Prefecture and a National Natural Monument since 1932. Free, on open shrine ground.
meta_description: Shinmeisha no Oshii in Nishio: a chinquapin of about 1,000 years, main trunk dead, secondary trunks still growing, 20 metres round at the roots.
question_meta: Nishio's only mapped tree is Shinmeisha no Oshii, a chinquapin put at about 1,000 years old at Kaminagara Shinmeisha, free to visit.
question_answer: Nishio's oldest and only mapped tree is Shinmeisha no Oshii, an evergreen chinquapin put at about a thousand years old, standing in front of the main hall of Kaminagara Shinmeisha in Kaminagara-cho, Nishio, Aichi Prefecture. It has been a National Natural Monument since 1932.
question_context: The tree is a survival rather than an intact veteran, and the sources say so plainly. Its original main trunk has died. Two secondary trunks of about a metre round each, plus suckers sprouting from the root around the base, now carry the crown, and both the national register and Nishio's own tourism listing describe that growth as vigorous and still extending upward. The figures are what you would expect of a tree rebuilt from its own base: about 20 metres of root circumference, seven metres round at chest height in the city's record and roughly eight in the register's, and a height of only eight metres. It is described as the largest sudajii, or Japanese chinquapin, in Aichi Prefecture, and it has been protected nationally since 19 April 1932. The thousand-year age is an estimate with no planting record behind it, so it is given as a round figure rather than a date; anyone who knows of a proper dating is welcome to send it. Visiting is simple. The tree stands directly in front of the shrine's main hall on open ground, free, with nothing between the path and the trunk.

trees.story:
The main trunk of this tree died. The tree did not.

Shinmeisha no Oshii stands directly in front of the main hall of Kaminagara Shinmeisha, an evergreen chinquapin put at about a thousand years old and described as the largest of its species in Aichi Prefecture. The original stem is gone as a working trunk. What took over is two secondary trunks of roughly a metre round each, together with a crowd of suckers thrown up from the root, and both the national register and Nishio's own listing describe that growth as thriving and still extending upward. The tree is younger than itself, in the part of it you can touch.

The measurements are as odd as that suggests. Twenty metres round at the roots, seven metres at chest height by the city's figure and about eight by the register's, and only eight metres tall. Wide, low and rebuilt from the base.

It has been a National Natural Monument since 19 April 1932, which means the state was already protecting it while the original trunk was failing. The thousand years is an estimate and nobody has a planting record; if you know of a dating, tell us.

Free, on open shrine ground, standing where anyone arriving at the hall has to look at it.
